endorsements.quote: To achieve the sustainable and equitable integration of LLMHS, it is essential to embed stakeholder-centric participatory approaches throughout the system lifecycle.

Incorporating stakeholder-centered methods, such as pre-design surveys and interviews, to identify and define specific healthcare problems early in the process ensures that solutions are not only innovative but also practically grounded.
Stakeholder involvement through co-design and iterative feedback sessions is essential to guarantee both the usability and efficacy of LLMHS.

Red Teaming 49 is a proactive participatory approach that involves stakeholders in ‘adversarial’ testing scenarios (e.g., presenting ambiguous or conflicting patient data to assess whether the system generates unsafe, biased, or inequitable clinical recommendations) to identify vulnerabilities and failure cases.
Continuous monitoring and feedback mechanisms should be established to collect usage data and performance metrics, including system accuracy, user behaviors, workflow impact, and patient outcomes.
By offering tailored learning modules specific to different roles and simulating healthcare scenarios, LLMs can facilitate hands-on practice that deepens understanding and builds confidence 63 .

Workflow designs must also include explicit verification points where clinicians can review and adjust AI-generated suggestions, thereby ensuring both efficiency and safety.
Stakeholder-engaged output validation is crucial in this context to ensure content accuracy, cultural alignment, and optimize readability.
Clinical Trials 13 : Validates efficacy and safety through controlled, real-world studies.

unlisted_practices: Define clear metrics for success, such as stakeholder satisfaction, reduction in model bias, and improved patient outcomes, for participatory LLM health system solutions.
Address the digital divide through offline functionality, low-bandwidth support, and partnerships with local communities to enhance technology access.
Co-design benchmarks and evaluation metrics with stakeholders, and report bias, toxicity, calibration, and deployment metrics in addition to accuracy.
Have stakeholders verify and contextualize synthetic data used for preliminary benchmarking, acknowledging it may oversimplify clinical complexity and introduce bias.
Establish clear handoff protocols between AI agents and clinicians in high-stakes clinical settings.
Integrate regular feedback sessions on explainable AI outputs into existing clinical infrastructure such as quality improvement meetings, involving clinicians and AI ethics experts.
Use pilot testing and validation studies of new features to identify issues before full-scale deployment.
Provide targeted stakeholder education and support to clarify LLM-related risks for participants in red teaming and participatory auditing.
Apply safety constraints and guardrails, such as rule-based detection and blocking of inappropriate outputs, to mitigate bias for marginalized patients.
Use stakeholder-in-the-loop RLHF and fine-tuning for iterative post-deployment adaptation of health LLMs.

screen.reason: This is a conceptual/perspective review paper exploring participatory design and stakeholder engagement frameworks across the development lifecycle of LLM-enhanced health systems.
